brief.hulao.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, 'Biography of Dong Zhuo' and 'Biography of Lü Bu' · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter Five
brief.jiameng.adaptation: This chapter writes the "lamp-lit night battle" as a game beyond victory and defeat: the two fiercest spears must fight to the full, until the torches burn short, until the spears themselves begin to speak.
brief.jiameng.boss.loss: Too eager to find Zhang Fei a winning chance, you cut off what the spear was trying to say. Ma Chao shuts his door and sees no one.
brief.jiameng.boss.title: Jiameng Pass · The Lamp-Lit Night Battle
brief.jiameng.boss.why: Zhang Fei wants to fight his fill, and Ma Chao wants to carve a way out. Beneath two hundred torches, what you must count is not the exchanges—but when the two spears begin to respect each other.
brief.jiameng.boss.win: The torches burn low; two tigers come to respect each other. The spear of Xiliang has found a new direction, and Shu-Han gains another general.
brief.jiameng.lead: The defeated soldiers of the south of the Wei have reached the gates of Jiameng. When Zhang Fei hears that Ma Chao has come, he laughs three times—then has the oath he once swore against drink pressed beneath the corner of his desk.
brief.jiameng.record: After joining Zhang Lu, Ma Chao attacked Jiameng and fought Zhang Fei; the tale of their lamp-lit night duel is a famous passage of the Romance. Ma Chao later surrendered to Liu Bei, and Shu-Han gained a great general thereby.
brief.jiameng.skirmish.loss: The edge is blunted before the gates, and Ma Chao turns from assault to siege; the torches of the night battle cannot be lit.
brief.jiameng.skirmish.title: Baxi · Ma Dai Tests the Edge
brief.jiameng.skirmish.why: Ma Dai comes ahead of his brother to probe the pass's defenses, his blade-work solid and heavy. Win this test, and Ma Chao will deign to come challenge the gates himself.
brief.jiameng.skirmish.win: The probe is seen through, and Ma Dai withdraws his blade to his lines; the main act at Jiameng can begin.
brief.jiameng.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Ma Chao and Zhang Fei · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 65
brief.jiange.adaptation: This chapter makes Jiange a frontal victory: Zhong Hui's proclamations are his cheapest scaling ladders. Hold the wall, but also keep a flank watch for Zhang Yi—that is the next page's business.
brief.jiange.boss.loss: A feint draws off the sentries, the front thins to paper; on the day the pass falls, Jiang Wei can only clasp his fists toward Yinping.
brief.jiange.boss.title: Jiange · Proclamations and Cliffs
brief.jiange.boss.why: Zhong Hui presses the cliffs with numbers, alternating offers of surrender and outright assault. You must keep this wall standing whole, never turning back for any proclamation.
brief.jiange.boss.win: Zhong Hui, grain exhausted, talks of withdrawal and writes in his notes: 'The difficulty is this man.' Shu-Han wins one more winter.
brief.jiange.lead: One hundred eighty thousand men press on the Sword Gate, and Jiang Wei holds the pass by its cliffs. Zhong Hui's proclamations are finely written—but the arrows of Jiange know only the blood behind the words.
brief.jiange.record: Wei sent 180,000 men in three columns against Shu; Jiang Wei withdrew to hold Jiange. Zhong Hui could not break through; his supplies ran far and thin, and he talked of returning—whereupon Deng Ai crossed secretly by Yinping, and Mianzhu and Chengdu followed.
brief.jiange.skirmish.loss: The camps press against the pass and siege engines are hauled closer daily; no cliff is steep enough to bear being measured every day.
brief.jiange.skirmish.title: Baishui · Vanguard Before the Pass
brief.jiange.skirmish.why: The Wei vanguard must camp before the pass. Blunt its edge now, and the walls of Jiange gain time to be made whole.
brief.jiange.skirmish.win: The vanguard falls back and the walls are repaired; old Liao Hua leans on the battlements and closes his eyes for the first time in four years.
brief.jiange.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, biographies of Jiang Wei and Zhong Hui · Romance, chapter 116
brief.jieqiao.adaptation: This episode turns the vanguard crossbow formation into a readable rhythm: Qu Yi's shields and crossbows each have their beat. Count the beats, and the White Horses gain a second way to charge besides the half-crossing.
brief.jieqiao.boss.loss: The White Horses fall in rows at the half-crossing, and Gongsun Zan from then on trusts only high walls and deep moats. Zhao Yun's spear can only clear the road for retreat.
brief.jieqiao.boss.title: Jie Bridge · White Horses Against Iron Spears
brief.jieqiao.boss.why: Wen Chou anchors Yuan Shao's line, his spear heavy but his temper quick. You must make Gongsun Zan heed one piece of Zhao Yun's advice, and not stake every rider on a single charge.
brief.jieqiao.boss.win: Hebei's center retreats north of Jie Bridge, and Zhao Yun's name first stirs Youyan. The White Horse Volunteers are beaten but not scattered, and still have the strength to fight again.
brief.jieqiao.lead: Youzhou's White Horses are called the finest cavalry under heaven; Hebei's vanguard is called the finest crossbows. The two names meet on the two banks of Jie Bridge, with a river not wide between them.
brief.jieqiao.record: At the Battle of Jie Bridge, Yuan Shao's commander Qu Yi led eight hundred vanguard troops to break Gongsun Zan's White Horse Volunteers, crossbows thundering. Zhao Yun was in Gongsun Zan's army at the time, first showing his skill.
brief.jieqiao.skirmish.loss: The White Horses bunch together on the riverbank, and the vanguard's crossbows spare no one. Broken at the half-crossing, Jie Bridge loses the first round.
brief.jieqiao.skirmish.title: Jie Bridge · The Vanguard Blocks the Way
brief.jieqiao.skirmish.why: Qu Yi's eight hundred raise their crossbows before any horse is seen. You must first count the rhythm of shield-down and crossbow-up, then decide in what formation the White Horses cross the river.
brief.jieqiao.skirmish.win: The vanguard's beat is noted, and the White Horse detachments have a basis for their route. Wen Chou's iron spear loses the advantage of waiting at ease.
brief.jieqiao.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Yuan Shao, Biography of Gongsun Zan · Book of the Later Han
brief.jieting.adaptation: This chapter gives both Ma Su and Wang Ping a voice, not reducing the failure to a single phrase about 'armchair strategy.' What you must change is the shared error of orders, terrain, and appointment.
brief.jieting.boss.loss: No water on the mountain, and Jieting still falls. The errors of Ma Su and Zhuge Liang are settled together; the empty city that follows leaves only a more desperate retreat.
brief.jieting.boss.title: Jieting · High Ground Is No Match for Long Water
brief.jieting.boss.why: Zhang He need not attack uphill; he need only surround the water and wait for your ranks to break. You must make Ma Su swallow his pride and pitch camp on the road before Zhang He closes the ring.
brief.jieting.boss.win: Jieting holds. Ma Su and Wang Ping rewrite the orders together, and Zhuge Liang need not shed tears—though the sound of a lute at Xicheng is about to rise.
brief.jieting.lead: If the road from Qishan is to last, it cannot break at Jieting. The more a man knows the manuals, the more he may stake a whole army's lives on a single rule.
brief.jieting.record: At the Battle of Jieting, Ma Su abandoned water to camp on the mountain and mishandled his troops; Zhang He cut off his water supply and defeated him, while Wang Ping's unit gathered the remnants. Zhuge Liang then executed Ma Su to answer to the army.
brief.jieting.skirmish.loss: The troops are drawn off the road, water and camp separated. Before Zhang He even arrives, the defenders have written their own tell.
brief.jieting.skirmish.title: Lieliu City · Vanguard Contests the Road
brief.jieting.skirmish.why: The Wei vanguard deliberately shows a gap in the supply route, but its real target is the water source below the mountain. Lured off the main road, Jieting loses its reason to be defended.
brief.jieting.skirmish.win: The vanguard's feint is seen through. Ma Su and Wang Ping survey the water route together, and there is still time to revise the orders for holding camp.
brief.jieting.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Zhuge Liang, Zhang He, and Wang Ping
brief.kongcheng.adaptation: This chapter openly adopts the Empty Fort Stratagem, writing Sima Yi's paranoia as a betting psychology that can be exploited. The victory is not that "he was too stupid," but that he chose the cheaper risk.
brief.kongcheng.boss.loss: The Wei army enters. The empty city has no soldiers to fight. Once a bluff is called, every old man and child in the original record pays the price.
brief.kongcheng.boss.title: Xicheng · One Lute, One Doubt
brief.kongcheng.boss.why: Sima Yi must decide which is cheaper: entering the city and being wrong, or retreating and missing his chance. You must make his deep thinking a second wall—not do his genius for him.
brief.kongcheng.boss.win: The lute never falters, the Wei army withdraws, and the old and weak within the city win time to evacuate. The fortified walls of Wuzhang Plains will be his next answer.
brief.kongcheng.lead: The answer at Jieting decides how many men remain at Xicheng—and how many real chips Zhuge Liang still has for a bluff with no bottom.
brief.kongcheng.record: After the defeat at Jieting, the Shu army withdrew to Hanzhong. Sima Yi being turned back by the empty city at Xicheng is not found in the main text of the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and the relevant Pei commentary has long been disputed. It is best treated as a famous story rather than established history.
brief.kongcheng.skirmish.loss: The truth is seen through first. The Wei army no longer weighs the cost of an ambush; the stratagem fails before Zhuge Liang ever touches the strings.
brief.kongcheng.skirmish.title: Xie Valley · Scouts Read the City
brief.kongcheng.skirmish.why: Wei scouts must first confirm whether the city is real or empty. If they see true panic, the gates and the lute are merely decorations inviting the enemy in.
brief.kongcheng.skirmish.win: The scouts bring back only contradictory clues. Sima Yi must enter the game carrying his doubts himself, and only then does the empty city have a chance of holding.
brief.kongcheng.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Zhuge Liang (Pei Songzhi's commentary); Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 95
brief.luofengpo.adaptation: This chapter keeps the Falling Phoenix Slope and the ambush, but trades the 'unlucky place-name' for real risks of route, mount, and lurking troops—so fate does not make the decision for the man.
brief.luofengpo.boss.loss: The stray arrow still falls before the slope, and the Fledgling Phoenix returns to the original scroll; you learn that so-called fate is often just a road no one thought to check again.
brief.luofengpo.boss.title: Falling Phoenix Slope · Dilu Not Swapped
brief.luofengpo.boss.why: Zhang Ren is waiting for precisely that familiar banner and mount. You must break his read on the route and the man, so the Fledgling Phoenix does not become the recognized target.
brief.luofengpo.boss.win: The ambush closes on empty ground, and Pang Tong pushes on toward Chengdu; the future of Ji Han no longer rests on the Crouching Dragon's shoulders alone.
brief.luofengpo.lead: The quarrel over Jing Province is not yet settled when the army into Shu arrives at Luo City. A man ranked with the Crouching Dragon yields the high road to his lord and keeps the narrow path for himself.
brief.luofengpo.record: When Liu Bei advanced into Yi Province, Pang Tong accompanied the army besieging Luo County and died of a stray arrow, aged thirty-six. The Falling Phoenix Slope, the swapping of mounts onto Dilu, and the ambush are flourishes the Romance piles on.
brief.luofengpo.skirmish.loss: The decoy troops drag the column into a narrow gorge, and every later realization becomes a pause before the arrow-storm.
brief.luofengpo.skirmish.title: Luo City · Shadows Before the Ambush
brief.luofengpo.skirmish.why: The Xi Chuan ambushers let a few figures show on purpose, luring you deep along the mountain track that looks most like a shortcut. Tell true from false first; only then can you speak of changing course.
brief.luofengpo.skirmish.win: The ambush layout is spotted in advance, and Pang Tong need not decide his advance or retreat on a place-name alone; Luo City still has more than one way in.
brief.luofengpo.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Pang Tong · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 63
brief.maicheng.adaptation: Lü Meng and Lu Xun share the table, and the white-clad and all-bluff rules drive home the rear's concealment. You may get Guan Yu out, but saving one man does not automatically repair the whole Jing Province line.
brief.maicheng.boss.loss: Snow falls on Maicheng, and Guan Yu still dies at Linju; the original scroll's unbearable regret comes to pass once more, and the Lesson will keep the clue of the white-clad feint.
brief.maicheng.boss.title: Maicheng · Two Schemes on a Snowy Night
brief.maicheng.boss.why: Lü Meng hides his edge, Lu Xun calculates deep, and together they want you watching only Guan Yu's valor while forgetting the city's supply. Win against both schemes, and only then can you contend for a road out.
brief.maicheng.boss.win: Yunchang fights free, and the old pages of Jing Province and Yiling change with him; the Great Pass apocrypha is stamped, and Volume Four opens early.
brief.maicheng.lead: The louder the victory at the Mian River, the deeper the emptiness at Jiangling. The greatest name and the coldest snow are one scroll apart; you must see the front's glory and the door at his back at once.
brief.maicheng.record: Lü Meng seized Jing Province while Guan Yu was north, and Gong'an and Jiangling fell in turn. Guan Yu withdrew to Maicheng and was later captured and killed at Linju; Sun Quan sent his head to Cao Cao.
brief.maicheng.skirmish.loss: The beacons fall silent and the road home is severed; the front-line hero becomes the last to know the rear is lost.
brief.maicheng.skirmish.title: Jiangling and Linju · White Cloth Cuts the Rear
brief.maicheng.skirmish.why: Wu's ambushers wear white instead of armor and cut the beacon chain and the way home first. Without rebuilding the message line, Guan Yu may be the last to learn that Jing Province has already fallen.
brief.maicheng.skirmish.win: Ambush and blockade are torn open, Maicheng is no longer an isolated city, and a direction for relief reappears between Shangyong and Jiangling.
brief.maicheng.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Guan Yu, the Lord of Wu, and Lü Meng
brief.nanjun.adaptation: This chapter writes Cao Ren's defense as a craft of "waiting for you to lose your temper": the drums on the wall are beaten solely for Zhou Yu's wound. You must count the Commander's relief rotations for him—not his provocations.
brief.nanjun.boss.loss: The wound splits from rage, and the tiger general storms the walls injured; the city may yet fall, but the Commander's fate is paid first.
brief.nanjun.boss.title: Jiangling · The Wound and the Drum
brief.nanjun.boss.why: Cao Ren's drum strikes only at Zhou Yu's anger and his wound. You must make the Commander record every provocation as the moment Cao's army changes its guard.
brief.nanjun.boss.win: Jiangling's gates open, and the arrow wound has not split; Zhou Yu strikes the drum three times and sends it back to Cao Ren—Nan Commandery passes to Wu, and the Commander's years are not cut short.
brief.nanjun.lead: The fires of Red Cliffs have barely died, yet every banner in Jing Province still bears the name of Cao. Zhou Yu, his arrow wound unhealed, commands from the riverbank, while atop the walls of Jiangling Cao Ren has already prepared a drum meant only to enrage him.
brief.nanjun.record: Zhou Yu besieged Nan Commandery for over a year, first sending Gan Ning to take Yiling, and rose to rally his troops even after taking a stray arrow; Cao Ren abandoned Jiangling and fled, and Nan Commandery passed to Wu. From this wound the Commander's arrow-scar would flare again and again.
brief.nanjun.skirmish.loss: Yiling holds, and the Wu army dares not divide its forces; Cao Ren is free to focus beneath Jiangling's walls and wear Zhou Yu down in a war of attrition.
brief.nanjun.skirmish.title: Yiling · The Road of Retreat
brief.nanjun.skirmish.why: Cao Hong holds the mouth of the Yiling road; if the Wu army is to split off and take the city, it must first pass this gate. Win here, and Gan Ning's bells can ring as far as Jiangling's flank.
brief.nanjun.skirmish.win: The Yiling road opens, and the Wu army advances by water and land; Jiangling's flank is checked, and Cao Ren has only the front to work with.
brief.nanjun.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Zhou Yu and Cao Ren · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 51
brief.qianli.adaptation: This chapter adopts the Romance's five passes and condenses them into five linked battles. The war chest travels all the way; each pass makes clear why its commander blocks the way and the price of letting you through.
brief.qianli.boss.loss: One position stalls, and war chest and road home break together. The whole scroll must start over; the passes already crossed won't hold your advantage for you.
brief.qianli.boss.title: Five Passes · A Thousand-Li Oath
brief.qianli.boss.why: Each of the five passes keeps its own orders; Guan Yu must hold to his old oath without letting his followers die on the road. Only by breaking five lines in a row can the way home be walked to its end.
brief.qianli.boss.win: All five passes cleared, the drums of Gucheng echo ahead. This rewrite isn't about killing a few more men — it's that the return home no longer bleeds you dry at every gate.
brief.qianli.lead: An identity forged at the green-plum pavilion cannot stay hidden forever. Guan Yu returns all he was given and sets out bearing an old oath; you must keep a thousand-li road from being cut short at every pass.
brief.qianli.record: That Guan Yu left Cao Cao and returned to Liu Bei is historical; the five passes—Dongling, Luoyang, and the rest—and the six officers such as Kong Xiu come mainly from the Romance, and must not be taken together as the historical route.
brief.qianli.skirmish.loss: The journey home halts outside Xudu; passage and honor cannot both be kept, and the thousand-li resolve falls first to a single sheet of paper.
brief.qianli.skirmish.title: Outskirts of Xudu · The First Roadblock
brief.qianli.skirmish.why: The pass commander wants your loyalty in exchange for transit papers. Guan Yu has already hung up his seal and returned his gold; he can no longer open the road with Cao Cao's authority.
brief.qianli.skirmish.win: The first roadblock is passed; carts, horses, and followers move east, and the five linked battles truly begin.
brief.qianli.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Guan Yu; Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapters 26–28
brief.qiqin.adaptation: The seven battles are not seven repeated victories, but seven stages of Meng Huo's attitude from fury to self-questioning. Each battle's Challenge changes, and victory or defeat must leave room for the next release.
brief.qiqin.boss.loss: You counted only the captures and releases, never deepening anyone's understanding. Restart the chapter; Nanzhong still does not believe in this 'Goading.'
brief.qiqin.boss.title: Nanzhong · Seven Captures, Seven Releases
brief.qiqin.boss.why: Meng Huo defends his dignity and his people's by refusing to submit. You must win seven times and release him six, so that in the end he yields to a choice, not to helplessness.
brief.qiqin.boss.win: Meng Huo himself sets the course for Nanzhong's tomorrow. The southern campaign turns from subjugation into a lasting pact, and Zhuge Liang can turn his army north.
brief.qiqin.lead: After Yong'an, Nanzhong rises again. Win only a surrender tablet, and the king you capture today will return tomorrow with more men.
brief.qiqin.record: In the third year of Jianxing, Zhuge Liang campaigns south and pacifies Nanzhong. The 'seven captures and seven releases' appear in Pei's commentary quoting Han-Jin Spring and Autumn; details such as rattan armor and poisonous springs are largely later literary expansions.
brief.qiqin.skirmish.loss: Lushui becomes a slaughter, and Meng Huo sees only another army come to conquer. The seven captures and releases lose their meaning before they begin.
brief.qiqin.skirmish.title: Lushui · Rattan Armor in the Way
brief.qiqin.skirmish.why: The rattan-armored troops hold the ford by terrain and gear. A forced crossing would turn the southern campaign into a blood feud where neither side will hear explanations.
brief.qiqin.skirmish.win: The ford opens, yet the captives are not cut down wholesale. The elders of Nanzhong speak of salt, grain, and old customs—and Goading gains facts to stand on.
brief.qiqin.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Zhuge Liang, Pei Songzhi's commentary quoting Han-Jin Spring and Autumn · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, southern campaign chapters
brief.qishan.adaptation: Cao Zhen represents Wei's strategy of waiting at ease for the exhausted enemy; supply lines and blinds represent long-term attrition. What you fight for here is a sustainable advance, not a blaze of glory.
brief.qishan.boss.loss: Supplies run out and the road is cut. The Memorial on Dispatching the Army is blown back onto the desk; the campaign is still written as a knowing waste.
brief.qishan.boss.title: Qishan · The Long Road Against the Wall
brief.qishan.boss.why: Cao Zhen means to grind your war chest empty with mountains and time. You must move supply lines, feints, and marching pace forward together until his wall means nothing.
brief.qishan.boss.win: The long road from Qishan is walked through. The northern campaign is no longer only a tragic slogan; Jieting now becomes the key fulcrum on that road.
brief.qishan.lead: With Nanzhong settled, the northern campaign finally has a rear. But however resolute the Memorial on Dispatching the Army, grain carts still must cross the mountains one by one, and soldiers cannot feed on a famous text.
brief.qishan.record: After the Memorial on Dispatching the Army, Zhuge Liang stations at Hanzhong and launches repeated northern expeditions; the routes and number do not match the popular 'Six Campaigns from Qishan.' This chapter is the northern campaign as a whole, not a reenactment of a single battle.
brief.qishan.skirmish.loss: The mountain roads are cut. The deeper the vanguard advances, the less retreat it has; 'advance' becomes staking the whole army on one supply run.
brief.qishan.skirmish.title: Hanzhong · Outposts and Supply Stations
brief.qishan.skirmish.why: Wei outposts strike at mountain roads and grain convoys. Guard only the commander's banner and not the supply stations, and the first march from Qishan will be the last.
brief.qishan.skirmish.win: The outposts are pinned down, supply stations link up along the route, and the northern campaign gains a foundation to return next year.
brief.qishan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Zhuge Liang · later narratives of the 'Six Campaigns from Qishan'
brief.ruxu.adaptation: This chapter writes the raid of the hundred riders as a war of eyes and ears: Cao's four hundred thousand do not lose to a hundred riders—they lose to not knowing how many riders have come.
brief.ruxu.boss.loss: The bells ring too early, and the panic in the camp wakes; the string of bells that comes back is thirty short from that day on.
brief.ruxu.boss.title: Ruxu Fort · The Bell Rings Thrice
brief.ruxu.boss.why: Cao Cao spreads his doubt across four hundred thousand men, and leaves a tell in every doubt. You must make the bells ring from a direction Cao Cao cannot imagine.
brief.ruxu.boss.win: The hundred riders return, not a single bell missing; Cao Cao sighs that "Sun Quan is not to be rushed," and withdraws his army to Xu.
brief.ruxu.lead: The campfires of four hundred thousand turn the river's face to daylight. On Sun Quan's desk lie a hundred bronze bells—what Xingba means to borrow is not the darkness, but Cao Cao's doubt.
brief.ruxu.record: Cao Cao, claiming four hundred thousand, attacked Ruxu; Gan Ning led a hundred riders in a night raid on Cao's camp, cut down the enemy, and returned without losing a single man. Sun Quan said: Mengde has Zhang Liao, and I have Xingba—they are a match for each other.
brief.ruxu.skirmish.loss: The outpost falls, and the Wu army is forced back behind its walls; the bells have not yet rung, and already the right to sally has been lost.
brief.ruxu.skirmish.title: Wankou · Yue Jin's Edge
brief.ruxu.skirmish.why: The Wei vanguard Yue Jin is a veteran of first assaults and means to charge while the Wu army is still gathering. Hold him, and the hundred riders in the fort can receive their orders to ride out.
brief.ruxu.skirmish.win: The vanguard's momentum is checked, and Ruxu Fort stands firm; at last the order for the hundred riders is placed in Gan Ning's hands.
brief.ruxu.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Gan Ning and the Sovereign of Wu · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 68
brief.sangu.adaptation: The three visits become three different tests. You press on after the first two failures not because Kongming is playing coy, but because you must prove that seeking talent means more than accepting a compliant answer.
brief.sangu.boss.loss: The third visit leaves only footprints outside the door, and the meeting in the original scroll is postponed. You must ask again what seeking talent truly seeks.
brief.sangu.boss.title: Wolong Ridge · Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage
brief.sangu.boss.why: Zhuge Liang isn't testing the formality of three knocks, but whether you can still listen carefully to a plan that won't flatter after repeated cold shoulders.
brief.sangu.boss.win: The cottage door opens, and the Longzhong Plan becomes a road you can walk. Jing, Yi, and the alliance with Wu are no longer just drunken boasts.
brief.sangu.lead: After Guandu, the north settles, yet Liu Bei, sheltering in Xinye, still lacks a long road forward. The answer lies not in a million-man war chest, but in a thatched cottage.
brief.sangu.record: On Xu Shu's recommendation, Liu Bei visited Zhuge Liang and saw him only on the third call. The Longzhong Plan laid out holding Jing and Yi, allying with Wu against Cao. The three visits are documented; the snow, the wind, and the rest are literary embellishment.
brief.sangu.skirmish.loss: You treat the search for talent as a task to be ticked off, and the boy reports only that the master is out. This visit never reaches the question itself.
brief.sangu.skirmish.title: Xinye · Asking the Way at Longzhong
brief.sangu.skirmish.why: The boy at the gate of Longzhong first asks whether you come for fame or for the realm. If you can't answer a doorkeeper's question, the cottage won't open for you.
brief.sangu.skirmish.win: You set aside your haste to "bring him out at any cost" and take the mountain path for another visit. The real test now shifts from the boy to the Crouching Dragon.
brief.sangu.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Zhuge Liang · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapters 37–38
brief.sanqi.adaptation: This chapter uses the Romance's three clashes to write Zhou Yu's temper and his arrow wound, without simply attributing his real death by illness to being angered to death by Zhuge Liang.
brief.sanqi.boss.loss: Arrow wound and rage snap as one, and the original scroll's 'since heaven made Yu' becomes a eulogy once more; you win the ground but fail to change the man.
brief.sanqi.boss.title: Baqiu · The Third Provocation
brief.sanqi.boss.why: Zhou Yu means to prove he can still hold the tiller of Jiangdong. You must see through his hot fury to the arrow wound and the pride beneath it, and decide whether this hand can be won only by striking at the sick and the weak.
brief.sanqi.boss.win: By the third burst he sees his own fixation clearly instead; Baqiu ceases to be merely a place of death, and the struggle over Jing and Xiang gains a road the record never finished.
brief.sanqi.lead: After Cao Cao turns north, the Sun-Liu alliance immediately faces the question of Jingzhou. Old friend and rival sit one seat apart, and the hardest thing is to contest the land without driving a man into a corner.
brief.sanqi.record: Zhou Yu died of illness at Baqiu in the fifteenth year of Jian'an at only thirty-six, still planning a campaign into Ba and Shu. 'Three times provoking Zhou Yu' and 'Since heaven made Yu, why make Liang?' are Romance inventions.
brief.sanqi.skirmish.loss: Scattered clashes confirm mutual suspicion, and all Zhou Yu receives is provocation. The negotiation turns into goading before it even begins.
brief.sanqi.skirmish.title: Nan Commandery · A New Crack in the Alliance
brief.sanqi.skirmish.why: Wu's young officers treat the old merit of Red Cliffs as a claim to land. If you fight only for the momentary upper hand in words, the alliance will break first at the frontier.
brief.sanqi.skirmish.win: The frontier dispute is held down for now, and Zhou Yu is willing to take a seat himself. The Jingzhou question can finally be discussed without young officers carrying messages.
brief.sanqi.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Zhou Yu · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapters 51–56
brief.shangfanggu.adaptation: This chapter gives this famous "act of Heaven" a chance to fight back: the rain will surely come, but whether fire or rain comes first depends on how fast the cards are played.
brief.shangfanggu.boss.loss: The rain beats the fire by half a quarter hour. Father and son laugh in the downpour; men did all they could, but the Omen turned first.
brief.shangfanggu.boss.title: Shangfang Valley · Fire and Rain
brief.shangfanggu.boss.why: Sima Yi's caution and Sima Zhao's eagerness split their force at the same valley mouth. You must set father and son half a day out of step—and raise the fire before the rain.
brief.shangfanggu.boss.win: The fire burns out, the work is done, and the rain falls after the fact. The Sima clan shuts its gates and stays shut; the autumn harvest south of the Wei goes to Shu.
brief.shangfanggu.lead: The ice on the Wei River melts and freezes again. The Shu army farms, the Wei army builds ramparts, and the two forces plant the same autumn harvest across the water from each other. And the dry wood piled at the valley mouth waits only for a man willing to walk in.
brief.shangfanggu.record: The fire trap at Shangfang Valley (Gourd Valley) is a Romance episode: Wei Yan lures Sima Yi and his sons into the valley, fire breaks out, and a great rain falls; father and sons escape. The histories contain no such event—only the standoff by the Wei River is true.
brief.shangfanggu.skirmish.loss: The grain road's secrets leak first; the bait is never set, and the shape of the trap shows. Sima Yi and his son dare not leave their ramparts at all.
brief.shangfanggu.skirmish.title: Wei River Bank · Scouts Between the Ramparts
brief.shangfanggu.skirmish.why: Wei scouts are probing for the Wooden Ox and the Flowing Horse. Win the fight for eyes on the grain road first—only then will anyone swallow the bait you left in the stores.
brief.shangfanggu.skirmish.win: With eyes on every road, the grain carts move inside your palm; the bait at Beiyuan hangs on the hook without a snag.
brief.shangfanggu.source: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 103 · Book of Jin, Annals of Emperor Xuan
brief.shenting.adaptation: This episode writes the duel as a hand that must be played to the full: victory is not in the number of rounds, but in whether both men have seen each other's true skill.
brief.shenting.boss.loss: You meddle in the duel and spoil it; the winner is unsatisfied, the loser resentful. The Lesson leaves one line: the spectator's hand overturns the table.
brief.shenting.boss.title: Shenting Ridge · Halberd Broken, Armor Torn
brief.shenting.boss.why: Taishi Ci does not seek to beat Sun Ce, only to play the whole hand through. You must hold back the hand that would decide for them, and let the two meet each other's true nature at the point of exhaustion.
brief.shenting.boss.win: The broken halberd and torn armor both become tokens of trust. No fight, no friendship: the spear of Donglai now knows the lord of Jiangdong.
brief.shenting.lead: Scouts report Sun Ce is probing the camp with only twelve riders, and Taishi Ci takes up his spear and gives chase. Others urge him to wait, and he says: chance and danger have always gone by the same name.
brief.shenting.record: Sun Ce campaigned against Liu Yao and fought Taishi Ci alone at Shenting Ridge, seizing his halberd and tearing his armor, with no victor decided. Taishi Ci was later cornered at Jing County and surrendered to Sun Ce, who clasped his hand and said, "Are the wise and cunning of the realm only one man?"
brief.shenting.skirmish.loss: The ridge road is sealed by military order, and the duel becomes a brawl. Neither weapon gets the dignity of a fair exchange.
brief.shenting.skirmish.title: Qu'a · The Guard Blocks the Way
brief.shenting.skirmish.why: Liu Yao's guards do not recognize Taishi Ci's solitary ways and seal off the ridge road first. For this fight to happen at all, you must make the men at the gate step aside.
brief.shenting.skirmish.win: The guards give way, and the soil of Shenting Ridge is left to the two men who truly want to cross weapons. The duel goes on without military orders spoiling it.
brief.shenting.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Taishi Ci, Biography of Sun Ce · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 15
brief.shezhan.adaptation: Zhang Zhao, Yu Fan, and Lu Ji question him from the same table, turning three stances into three poker styles. The goal is not to humiliate the civil officials, but to make resisting Cao seem anything other than doomed.
brief.shezhan.boss.loss: Many mouths melt metal. You are left with only the place of a supplicant, Jiangdong's agenda returns to avoiding war, and the coalition to resist Cao in the original record loses a measure of its strength.
brief.shezhan.boss.title: Council Hall · Three Scholars at One Table
brief.shezhan.boss.why: Zhang Zhao asks about the great tide, Yu Fan about your defeats, Lu Ji about your foundations. You must answer each in turn without letting the three close in and speak the same word: 'surrender.'
brief.shezhan.boss.win: The hall stops letting numbers of voices stand in for judgment, and Sun Quan hears that resisting Cao may still have a chance. The next scheme begins to take shape in the river fog.
brief.shezhan.lead: After Changban, Liu Bei can no longer hold Cao Cao off alone. Every word of 'surrender' or 'fight' in Jiangdong decides whether his battered army still has somewhere to stand.
brief.shezhan.record: After Cao Cao moves south, Zhuge Liang is sent to Jiangdong to meet Sun Quan, where Lu Su, Zhou Yu, and others press hard for resisting Cao. The parade of scholars questioning him one by one, and Kongming debating them all single-handed, is one of the novel's most concentrated set pieces.
brief.shezhan.skirmish.loss: The talk at the post station settles it first: 'Cao cannot be opposed.' Every word you say after will be taken as a loser's dressing-up of a plea for help.
brief.shezhan.skirmish.title: Chaisang Post Station · Seizing the First Word
brief.shezhan.skirmish.why: The Jiangdong scholars open by weighing strength against weakness and pressing for surrender. If you have nothing but feeling, you have already admitted there is no way out before you ever enter the council hall.
brief.shezhan.skirmish.win: The first round of questioning is picked apart. You earn the right to enter the council hall and lay out the disaster in Jingzhou and the case for resisting Cao.
brief.shezhan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biographies of Zhuge Liang, Lu Su, and Zhou Yu · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 43
brief.shuiyan.adaptation: This chapter turns the autumn rains and high ground into pre-battle conditions. The flood is no miracle out of nowhere; what truly matters is who can use the Omen without being turned on by it.
brief.shuiyan.boss.loss: The rain stops before the dikes break, Yu Jin's formation stands intact, and Guan Yu loses his greatest chance; the empty rear in Jing Province is now a fact.
brief.shuiyan.boss.title: Mian River · Seven Armies All Fish
brief.shuiyan.boss.why: Yu Jin means to drag out the rainy season with an intact formation. You must force his choice between the dikes and the heights—not simply wait for the flood to win for you.
brief.shuiyan.boss.win: The seven armies are wiped out and Yu Jin taken; Guan Yu's name shakes Xudu. Yet Lü Meng's white-clad men are already slipping toward Jiangling.
brief.shuiyan.lead: Hanzhong decided, the northern push from Jing Province unfolds at the same time. Guan Yu is one rain away from shaking the realm, and only a few steps from zenith to decline.
brief.shuiyan.record: Days of heavy rain swelled the Han River, trapping the seven armies under Yu Jin's command. Yu Jin surrendered and Pang De was slain; Guan Yu's name 'shook the realm'—the height of his northern campaign.
brief.shuiyan.skirmish.loss: The rains trap your own maneuvering first, and the relief force cannot join; the so-called Omen turns into Cao's shield.
brief.shuiyan.skirmish.title: Fancheng · Beneath the Rain Line
brief.shuiyan.skirmish.why: Yu Jin's troops seize the high ground and the ford. If the passage is not taken before the water rises further, both the tower ships and the relief force will be cut off outside Fancheng.
brief.shuiyan.skirmish.win: Ford and heights are linked again, the seven armies' low camps lie exposed below the waterline, and Guan Yu holds the initiative.
brief.shuiyan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Guan Yu and Yu Jin
brief.sishui.adaptation: This chapter follows the Romance's 'Warm Wine, Slain Hua Xiong,' compressing the lords' contempt, Guan Yu's plea to fight, and a single cup of wine into one and the same poker table.
brief.sishui.boss.loss: The wine goes cold and the pass stands unbroken; the regret written in the record falls once more. You will learn that this table punishes being hurried by his winning streak.
brief.sishui.boss.title: Sishui Pass · The Wine Still Warm
brief.sishui.boss.why: Hua Xiong means to use his streak to force his opponent into a reckless charge, while Guan Yu must win himself one chance to fight without waiting for rank's permission.
brief.sishui.boss.win: Hua Xiong falls back, the wine has not cooled, and the lords can no longer measure a hero by birth alone; the halberd of Hulao Pass swings round to point at you.
brief.sishui.lead: The wine of the Peach Garden is still warm, yet the lords at Suanzao each harbor their own designs. The next cup must be carried back by hand by a man no one has heard of.
brief.sishui.record: In the first year of Chuping, the commanderies east of the Pass raised troops against Dong Zhuo. Hua Xiong was a general under Dong Zhuo, and was later defeated and slain by Sun Jian's army at the Battle of Yangren—not by Guan Yu.
brief.sishui.skirmish.loss: The alliance loses the first clash, and the command tent fills with nothing but men deferring to one another; Hua Xiong's winning streak keeps bearing down on every last name.
brief.sishui.skirmish.title: Suanzao · Before the Lords' Camp
brief.sishui.skirmish.why: The Xiliang riders are testing the alliance's nerve. If you cannot even hold back these raiders, Guan Yu will never get the chance to step before the command tent and ask to fight.
brief.sishui.skirmish.win: The outriders are driven back toward Sishui, the lords finally deign to listen to a mere mounted archer, and that cup of warm wine finds its master.
brief.sishui.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, 'Biography of Sun the Vanguard' · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter Five
brief.skirmishMeta: Met on the march · even defeat enters the record
brief.taoyuan.adaptation: The Peach Garden Oath follows the Romance narrative. The Writer seats you among them as a fellow traveler, and your first task is to win the town militia and those three old friends a road they can walk together, advancing or retreating as one.
brief.taoyuan.boss.loss: The Yellow Turban tide still spreads as the record foretold, and the oath so newly sworn is torn apart by the rebel horde; even in defeat, Lessons remain of rescuing one another and covering the retreat.
brief.taoyuan.boss.title: Guangzong · The Rebel Chief's Table
brief.taoyuan.boss.why: The rebel chief leans on the sheer weight of his rabble to overwhelm this freshly gathered band. Only by driving him from the table can the militia truly find its footing.
brief.taoyuan.boss.win: The Peach Garden oath has weathered its first defeat, and the apocrypha is sealed with its mark; you will follow the beacon smoke of the lords' alliance onward to Sishui.
brief.taoyuan.lead: The tattered scroll's first page holds no emperor—only a recruitment notice soaked through by rain. You must first understand why heroes would entrust their lives to one another.
brief.taoyuan.record: In the first year of Zhongping the Yellow Turbans rose. Liu Bei gathered local militia in Zhuo Commandery and joined the government forces in putting them down. The age of chaos did not begin with the Three Kingdoms' tripartite stand; it began with countless commanderies and counties scrambling to defend themselves.
brief.taoyuan.skirmish.loss: The militia is scattered. Before the oath in the peach garden is even sworn, you learn the price of each man fighting alone; this page returns to the record, and you begin again with the Lesson in hand.
brief.taoyuan.skirmish.title: Zhuo Commandery · The Militia's First Stand
brief.taoyuan.skirmish.why: Yellow Turban raiders are closing on the village road, and the new recruits have yet to form ranks. You must head off their vanguard first, so the militia has time to shield the people and keep the line of retreat open.
brief.taoyuan.skirmish.win: The village road holds. The militia is willing to follow you on to the peach grove, and three strangers have found their first taste of trust fighting shoulder to shoulder.
brief.taoyuan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, 'Biography of the First Sovereign' · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter One
brief.tianshui.adaptation: This chapter frames the winning of Jiang Wei as a game of "invitation": his edge comes from having read all the Chancellor's old drafts, and you must use those same drafts to lock him down, then let the Chancellor offer the letter.
brief.tianshui.boss.loss: Rushing to win him over, you are outplayed at your own game; his resolve to hold his land hardens, and the Chancellor must look for another heir.
brief.tianshui.boss.title: Tianshui · The Youth's First Move
brief.tianshui.boss.why: Jiang Wei's every step is the first move, because your every step has already been read by him. To win, make him see that what he truly means to defend is not Ma Zun's city.
brief.tianshui.boss.win: The youth bows to the ground, and the Shu camp gains a name that has read every draft of the Chancellor; the roster of the northern campaigns is rewritten.
brief.tianshui.lead: Three commanderies surrender at the first sign, but on the walls of Tianshui stands a youth who has seen through every one of the Chancellor's feints. Zhao Yun returns to camp and is silent a long while, then says only four words: that spearmanship has a source.
brief.tianshui.record: On Zhuge Liang's first campaign out of Qishan, Jiang Wei, a commandant of Tianshui, saw through the trick of luring the tiger from its mountain and instead set an ambush that badly defeated Zhao Yun; later, distrusted by Ma Zun, he surrendered to Shu. Liang said, "This man is the finest of Liang Province."
brief.tianshui.skirmish.loss: The commandery formation instead traps your vanguard; you cannot even meet his face, let alone win him over.
brief.tianshui.skirmish.title: Jicheng · The Commandery Formation
brief.tianshui.skirmish.why: The commandery troops' formation comes from Jiang Wei's hand; break the outer ring first, and you can look across the table at that youth.
brief.tianshui.skirmish.win: The outer ring broken, the gates of Jicheng open; Jiang Wei comes out himself to see the one who read his formation.
brief.tianshui.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Jiang Wei · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 93
brief.tielongshan.adaptation: This chapter takes the Romance's Iron Cage Mountain frame and sets victory and defeat outside the ring: whoever would cage the mountain must first win the roads beyond it—the Qiang, the grain road, and the word 'borrow' on Guo Huai's lips.
brief.tielongshan.boss.loss: The Qiang fire burns back into your own camp; the besieger is besieged, and Jiang Wei pulls back to Jiange with bitterness in his heart.
brief.tielongshan.boss.title: Iron Cage Mountain · The Ring and the Roads
brief.tielongshan.boss.why: Guo Huai will not wrestle your ring—he will take it apart. The Qiang road, the grain road, the water road: hold one of the three and the siege holds.
brief.tielongshan.boss.win: The Qiang road holds and the relief column comes to nothing; Sima Zhao sues for peace with his last waterskin and withdraws. The gates of Longyou open for Shu.
brief.tielongshan.lead: At the Tao River the Wei army lost tens of thousands. Iron Cage Mountain has no water, yet the men below are calm—because beyond the siege lines runs one more road: the road that borrows Qiang soldiers.
brief.tielongshan.record: Jiang Wei won a great victory west of the Tao River and laid siege to Didao; Wei sent Chen Tai and Guo Huai to break the siege. The Romance turns this campaign into Sima Zhao trapped on Iron Cage Mountain and Guo Huai struck by an arrow.
brief.tielongshan.skirmish.loss: A corner of the siege fence is torn open and morale wavers; Guo Huai's relief column has not come, but the siege loosens first.
brief.tielongshan.skirmish.title: Didao · Testing Zhao's Camp
brief.tielongshan.skirmish.why: Even a cornered beast will reach out a claw. Hold off the probing troops coming down the mountain, and the siege fences will stand firm.
brief.tielongshan.skirmish.win: The probe is beaten back and the mountain's water runs tighter still; the three-day pledge begins its countdown.
brief.tielongshan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, biographies of Jiang Wei and Guo Huai · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 109
brief.tongguan.adaptation: This chapter writes the stratagem of discord as a single ink blot on the table: Cao Cao and Jia Xu do not win by force of arms but by letting Ma Chao see that blot for himself. The Tiger Fool's courage merely buys the blot its time.
brief.tongguan.boss.loss: Iron cavalry breaks through the ice city, and cutting the beard and casting off the robe come true; the discord never lands, and the fury of Liang Province burns through the south of the Wei first.
brief.tongguan.boss.title: South of the Wei · Ma Chao and the Tiger Fool
brief.tongguan.boss.why: Ma Chao's anger is the source of your chips, and Xu Chu's courage is the wall that stops the arrows. You must let that ink blot on the letter fall exactly where Ma Chao can see it.
brief.tongguan.boss.win: The Xiliang army scatters in mutual suspicion, and Cao Cao strokes his beard and smiles; Ma Chao rides west alone, his hatred undimmed but his direction lost.
brief.tongguan.lead: In the sandstorm of Tong Pass stands a white-robed figure with a silver spear. As Ma Chao stakes his father's vengeance on the table, in Cao Cao's command tent Jia Xu slowly grinds his ink—but it is no challenge he is grinding.
brief.tongguan.record: Ma Chao and Han Sui raised ten tribes of Xiliang in revolt; Cao Cao used Jia Xu's stratagem of sowing discord, and Chao and Sui, each suspecting the other, were defeated. The tales of cutting his beard and casting off his robe, and of Xu Chu stripping his armor to duel Ma Chao, are embellishments of the Romance.
brief.tongguan.skirmish.loss: Pang De breaks camp after camp, and Cao Cao is forced to draw up his lines with a river at his back; the ink of discord has not yet been ground, and already it must see blood.
brief.tongguan.skirmish.title: Tong Pass · Pang De Leads
brief.tongguan.skirmish.why: Ma Chao's vanguard Pang De has a heavy blade and a settled will; win this first bout, and Cao Cao's camp south of the Wei will have room to build its ramparts at leisure.
brief.tongguan.skirmish.win: The vanguard is checked, and the Xiliang spearhead draws in a little; the time to freeze the Wei and raise the ramparts is bought with your own hands.
brief.tongguan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of Ma Chao, Emperor Wu, and Jia Xu · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 58
brief.wancheng.adaptation: This chapter makes Dian Wei's twin halberds and the rear-camp escape route the heart of the Challenge. Hu Che'er stealing the halberds and similar details follow the novel, giving you a chance to hold that night.
brief.wancheng.boss.loss: The gate is still held by Dian Wei at the cost of his life; the record's wounds and deaths are all kept. The Lesson will leave its warning about weapons and escape routes.
brief.wancheng.boss.title: Wancheng · The Twin Halberds Unlost
brief.wancheng.boss.why: Zhang Xiu wants back the dignity of being slighted; Cao Cao needs a chance to leave the camp alive. You must make Dian Wei the gate, not trade his life for time.
brief.wancheng.boss.win: The twin halberds still stand, the gate is unbroken; Dian Wei and Cao Cao both walk out of the fire. The White Gate Tower at Xiapi follows.
brief.wancheng.lead: The gate saved Xiaopei, but not every slight can be saved. At Wancheng Cao Cao took surrender as silence; the night has already answered for the surrendered general.
brief.wancheng.record: Zhang Xiu surrendered and rebelled again, raiding Cao's camp by night. Dian Wei held the camp gate to the death; Cao Ang and Cao Anmin also perished. It was the price Cao Cao paid at Wancheng.
brief.wancheng.skirmish.loss: The stirring of the surrendered camp is taken for an ordinary night patrol; by the time fire reaches the gate, every escape route belongs to the ambush.
brief.wancheng.skirmish.title: Yu River · The Surrendered Camp Stirs
brief.wancheng.skirmish.why: Troops that surrendered by day regroup by night. You must tell whether they are being forced back to camp or have resolved to rebel, and leave Dian Wei a warning.
brief.wancheng.skirmish.win: The night movement is seen through in advance; the twin halberds and the horse road are both guarded, and Cao Cao no longer treats the banquet as absolute safety.
brief.wancheng.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Annals of Emperor Wu; Biography of Dian Wei
brief.wuzhangyuan.adaptation: This chapter keeps the fortified walls, the women's clothes, the soldier-farming, and the autumn wind, letting dwindling supplies and accelerating blinds close in together. You are to rewrite the falling star—not turn Sima Yi into a clown afraid to fight.
brief.wuzhangyuan.boss.loss: In the autumn wind the star falls as before. Sima Yi wins the endgame by waiting alone; this chapter's major gate does not change—the star falls, and still falls.
brief.wuzhangyuan.boss.title: Wuzhang Plains · Autumn Wind and Fortified Walls
brief.wuzhangyuan.boss.why: Sima Yi treats not fighting as the longest bet. You must make him pay for every refusal before the grain runs out—while preserving Zhuge Liang's time.
brief.wuzhangyuan.boss.win: The walls are pried open, the southeastern star still burns, and Zhuge Liang wins the years to keep writing the northern campaigns. The future of Gaopingling is shaken too.
brief.wuzhangyuan.lead: An empty city wins only once, by luck. At Wuzhang Plains there is no empty city to retreat behind. Both men have grown old; this time it is a contest of who still dares to live each day in earnest.
brief.wuzhangyuan.record: Zhuge Liang encamped at Wuzhang Plains and faced off against Sima Yi, dividing his troops to farm the land in hopes of a long stay. He then died in camp at fifty-four, and the Shu army withdrew. The northern campaigns end on this page.
brief.wuzhangyuan.skirmish.loss: The raiders scatter the defenders, and the granary and the medicine bowl run dry together. Before the fortified walls even speak, the autumn wind has already scored.
brief.wuzhangyuan.skirmish.title: Wugong River · Raiders Drain the Grain
brief.wuzhangyuan.skirmish.why: Wei raiders avoid battle, endlessly harassing the farms and supply lines. If you are led around putting out fires, Sima Yi wins without lifting a finger.
brief.wuzhangyuan.skirmish.win: The supply roads and farms hold. The Shu army need not rush to battle for a single meal; Zhuge Liang can finally count tomorrow into his plans.
brief.wuzhangyuan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Zhuge Liang; Book of Jin: Annals of Emperor Xuan
brief.xianshan.adaptation: In this episode, Huang Zu and Cai Mao share the same table. Huang Zu's one chance to beat Sun Jian lies entirely in the word "ambush"; you must read the arrows in the bamboo shadows for the tiger.
brief.xianshan.boss.loss: The tiger falls among the bamboo shadows, and Sun Ce takes up the banner of vengeance early. The Lesson will tell you: the tiger was lost to rage, not to courage.
brief.xianshan.boss.title: Mount Xian · Arrows and the Tiger
brief.xianshan.boss.why: Huang Zu means to finish Sun Jian with a storm of arrows and the terrain, while Cai Mao holds the water route of retreat. You must make the tiger slow down where the bamboo grows thick—without grinding down his will to fight.
brief.xianshan.boss.win: Sun Jian turns his horse around, and the foundation of Jiangdong is not broken at the opening stroke. Huang Zu breaks an arrow as his oath, and the struggle for Jingxiang is left to the next generation.
brief.xianshan.lead: The fires of Luoyang have not gone out, and the Imperial Seal is still tucked against Sun Jian's chest. Someone on the walls of Xiangyang has done the figures: a tiger is far more likely to die in pursuit than in a straight fight.
brief.xianshan.record: Sun Jian struck at Liu Biao and besieged Xiangyang. Riding alone up Mount Xian, he fell into an ambush and was killed by arrows and stone at the age of thirty-seven. The Romance attributes the ambush to Lü Gong's setup; Huang Zu had earlier been defeated by Sun Jian.
brief.xianshan.skirmish.loss: The vanguard is snagged by the bamboo shadows, and the formation scatters in pursuit. The ambushers at Mount Xian wait at ease while the main force is exhausted before battle.
brief.xianshan.skirmish.title: Deng Fort · Phantom Soldiers in the Bamboo
brief.xianshan.skirmish.why: Lü Gong's fleeing troops pass through the bamboo grove, their silhouettes mingled with the shadows. You must first tell whether this chaos is a real rout or an invitation into the trap before there can be any talk of pursuit.
brief.xianshan.skirmish.win: The bamboo shadows are seen through, the ambushers show themselves, and Sun Jian's vanguard no longer advances blindly. The main table at Mount Xian can unfold once you have read the ground clearly.
brief.xianshan.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Sun Jian · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 7
brief.xiaoyaojin.adaptation: This chapter makes the eight hundred warriors the embodiment of "seizing the chaos": every hand Zhang Liao wins is one the Wu army first threw into disorder. If a hundred thousand men hold their formation, eight hundred are just eight hundred.
brief.xiaoyaojin.boss.loss: The bridge breaks, and Ling Tong's three hundred guards are left on the far bank; the night weeping of Jiangdong now has a name.
brief.xiaoyaojin.boss.title: Xiaoyaojin · The Bridge at Mid-Crossing
brief.xiaoyaojin.boss.why: Zhang Liao's blade always falls where the Wu army is most disordered. Keep a hundred thousand men whole mid-crossing, and hold the retreat open for Ling Tong's rearguard.
brief.xiaoyaojin.boss.win: The ford is crossed safely, Ling Tong comes back; Zhang Liao sheathes his blade, and the men of Wu remember Hefei—and their own disorder.
brief.xiaoyaojin.lead: The gates of Hefei open without a sound; not a drop of water clings to the eight hundred men's armor—they have waited all night. Outside the walls, a hundred thousand Wu troops have just struck camp.
brief.xiaoyaojin.record: While Cao Cao campaigned against Zhang Lu, Zhang Liao, Li Dian, and Yue Jin held Hefei with seven thousand men. Liao led eight hundred in a charge that broke the enemy line; Sun Quan besieged the city for over ten days without success, and nearly was captured during the retreat. Hence "Zhang Liao stops the crying child."
brief.xiaoyaojin.skirmish.loss: Half the retreat is sealed by Li Dian, and the Wu army jams on the riverbank; before Zhang Liao even charges, the formation breaks itself.
brief.xiaoyaojin.skirmish.title: Shishui · Li Dian Holds Firm
brief.xiaoyaojin.skirmish.why: Li Dian arrays his troops with room to spare, sealing off the Wu army's retreat. Clear his gate first, and the planks of the ferry bridge will have time to be repaired.
brief.xiaoyaojin.skirmish.win: The line stands firm, the crossing proceeds in order; Sun Quan's center can form up intact.
brief.xiaoyaojin.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biographies of Zhang Liao and the Lord of Wu · Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 67
brief.yanglu.adaptation: This chapter brings the 'war without war' to the card table: Yang Hu's blade is trust, and a reckless attack plays straight into his hands. Take Xiling first, then honor the pact—that is Wu's last dignity.
brief.yanglu.boss.loss: The edict to press the attack drowns out the border's trust. On the day you march, the hearts of men have already crossed the river.
brief.yanglu.boss.title: Xiangyang · The Bond Across the Border
brief.yanglu.boss.why: Yang Hu baits with trust and hooks with virtue; his way of winning is 'not to fight.' You must win the same word—not the man.
brief.yanglu.boss.win: Xiling is settled, the border's trust intact; two steles face each other across the river, and neither man lost to the other.
brief.yanglu.lead: For two years the Jing Province border saw no fighting. A deer shot by Wu hunters fled into the Jin camp—and the Jin men truly sent it back. When Lu Kang fell ill, the medicine came from Xiangyang. Both sides were playing the same game: the hearts of men.
brief.yanglu.record: Yang Hu and Lu Kang faced each other across Jing Province. Yang Hu opened markets and built trust; envoys passed freely between them. Lu Kang said: 'He deals only in virtue, I deal only in force—that is to submit without a battle.' At Xiling, Lu Kang broke Bu Chan first, then turned back Yang Hu.
brief.yanglu.skirmish.loss: The gates fall, and Jianye grows ever more suspicious that Lu Kang is hoarding troops. The trust across the border loses first to your own city.
brief.yanglu.skirmish.title: Xiling · The Rebel City's Old Soldiers
brief.yanglu.skirmish.why: Bu Chan surrendered his city to Jin; his old soldiers hold the ramparts. Secure your own gates first, or the border's trust is a joke.
brief.yanglu.skirmish.win: The rebel city returns to Wu; all is settled within and without. Only now is a game with Lord Yang worthy of being called 'sitting across from one another.'
brief.yanglu.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Lu Kang / Book of Jin: Biography of Yang Hu — Romance, Chapter 120
brief.yiling.adaptation: This chapter writes vengeance, linked camps, and fire oil as a chain of risks. If Maicheng has been changed, Guan Yu himself will reject the pointless sacrifice made in his name—but war may still come.
brief.yiling.boss.loss: The fire races seven hundred li as the original record foretold. Liu Bei flees to Baidi; Yiling burns not only the camps but also the choices left to Shu Han.
brief.yiling.boss.title: Yiling · Before the Fire
brief.yiling.boss.why: Lu Xun feeds your impatience with his defenses and waits for your mistakes amid the linked camps. Before the blinds and your fury drain the army, you must let Liu Bei see the lives beyond the camp walls.
brief.yiling.boss.win: The old camps stand empty; the fire has nowhere to spread. The eastern campaign no longer ends in catastrophe—yet the sickbed at Yong'an Palace still waits for you.
brief.yiling.lead: The answer at Jing Province decides the reason for the eastern campaign, but cannot decide by itself how it is fought. Before fury burns men, it braids its own camps into a fuse.
brief.yiling.record: Liu Bei launched a great eastern campaign; Lu Xun first held fast and avoided his edge, then shattered Shu's camps by fire around Yiling and Xiaoting. Liu Bei withdrew to Baidi, and Ji Han was gravely weakened.
brief.yiling.skirmish.loss: The fire oil creeps close to the linked camps. The more the Shu troops counterattack, the more they stretch their lines—and Lu Xun has only to wait.
brief.yiling.skirmish.title: Zigui Xiaoting · Fire-Oil Outpost
brief.yiling.skirmish.why: The Wu fire-oil squads are testing your camp along the forest roads. Cut their fire paths first—don't treat every raid as an invitation to a decisive battle.
brief.yiling.skirmish.win: The fire-oil caches and forest paths are mapped. The Shu camp can now break apart its linked palisades, and Lu Xun loses his easiest fire.
brief.yiling.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biographies of the Former Lord and Lu Xun
brief.yinping.adaptation: This chapter writes the Yinping defenses as a chain of lamps watching one another. If Jieting has been changed, Ma Su will warn you from his own old mistake: height is not solid ground—grain, water, and communication are.
brief.yinping.boss.loss: Deng Ai passes through the unguarded places. Mianzhu and Chengdu are exposed in turn, and Shu-Han surrenders as originally written.
brief.yinping.boss.title: Mount Motian · Someone on the Dead-End Road
brief.yinping.boss.why: Deng Ai stakes his whole army on moving forward. You must prove with supply lines and mutually watching posts that a perilous road is no shortcut—and that landing does not mean victory.
brief.yinping.boss.win: The Yinping raid is intercepted. Jiangyou and Chengdu win a new line of defense; the final page of submission to Jin thus takes another possible shape.
brief.yinping.lead: After Gaopingling, the Sima clan's Wei finally reaches for Shu. Everyone says there is no road through Yinping—yet Deng Ai means to wrap "impossible" in old felt and roll it down the mountain.
brief.yinping.record: The Wei army invaded Shu. Deng Ai made a surprise march through the perilous Yinping road, crossed Mount Motian, took Jiangyou, then defeated Zhuge Zhan at Mianzhu and arrived before Chengdu, where Liu Shan surrendered.
brief.yinping.skirmish.loss: The beacons do not know whether one another still stand. When the surprise force lands, every city still believes the mountains will defend it on their own.
brief.yinping.skirmish.title: Tazhong-Yinping · The Surprise Force Has Not Landed
brief.yinping.skirmish.why: Deng Ai's surprise force trades retreat for speed. You must restore the beacon network before they land—not keep assuming a dead-end needs no guard.
brief.yinping.skirmish.win: The lamps on the cliffs connect. Jiangyou gains warning and time to move grain, and the surprise attack can no longer pierce straight to Chengdu's gate.
brief.yinping.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of Deng Ai; Biography of the Later Ruler
brief.yuanshemen.adaptation: This chapter keeps the historical frame of the arrow at the gate and turns the question of whether both sides honor the same wager into a card game: one arrow can break a siege, but the miss must be accounted for too.
brief.yuanshemen.boss.loss: The arrow-wager is never set. Ji Ling and Liu Bei each prepare for war; the mediator becomes a third creditor, and the record's draw never comes.
brief.yuanshemen.boss.title: The Gate · One Arrow, One Wager
brief.yuanshemen.boss.why: Ji Ling cannot withdraw a whole army over a performance. You must make him accept the wager, and force Lü Bu to say first what happens if the arrow misses.
brief.yuanshemen.boss.win: Both sides lay down arms and Xiaopei gains breathing room; Lü Bu proves he can untie a knot, not merely cut through it.
brief.yuanshemen.lead: Lü Bu, having left Meiwu, arrives at Xiaopei. A man who once knew only how to charge must now make two armies step back with a single arrow.
brief.yuanshemen.record: Yuan Shu sent Ji Ling to attack Liu Bei; Lü Bu set a feast to mediate, and made it the wager that his arrow would strike the small branch of the halberd at the camp gate. After the arrow struck, Ji Ling and the others withdrew their troops—a feat of archery that is recorded in the histories.
brief.yuanshemen.skirmish.loss: A misunderstanding turns to battle first; Xiaopei is dragged into the clash of two armies, and the arrow at the gate has no open ground left to land on.
brief.yuanshemen.skirmish.title: Xiaopei · Between Two Armies
brief.yuanshemen.skirmish.why: Ji Ling's troops are already pressing on Xiaopei; one mistaken charge could rob the mediation of its name. Hold the vanguard first, and only then can the banquet at the gate be set.
brief.yuanshemen.skirmish.win: Both sides halt the killing. Ji Ling agrees to enter the banquet under his commander's orders, and Liu Bei need not stake a whole city's people on one man's courage.
brief.yuanshemen.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, 'Biography of Lü Bu'
brief.zhujiu.adaptation: This chapter keeps the duel of judgment over heroes, letting Cao Cao wager by reading men; if the White Gate Tower has changed, he will still test you with a Lü Bu who did not die.
brief.zhujiu.boss.loss: Cao Cao reads fear in every call you make; the green-plum wine becomes an interrogation, and the record still lets him define what a hero is.
brief.zhujiu.boss.title: Green-Plum Pavilion · Heroes Drink
brief.zhujiu.boss.why: Cao Cao forces you to admit your ambition with a single word, "sovereign." You must hide your alarm and see clearly whether he is praising a man or pricing one.
brief.zhujiu.boss.win: The chopsticks fall but your heart does not; you leave Xudu with an answer no one has spoken aloud. On the next page, someone will hang up his seal and return his gold.
brief.zhujiu.lead: You come to Xudu with Xiapi's answer. Cao Cao no longer asks who can charge, only whom in your heart deserves to be called a hero.
brief.zhujiu.record: Cao Cao's words to Liu Bei, "the heroes of the realm today are you and I alone," appear in the Records. The green plums and wine, and the chopsticks dropped at the thunderclap, are elaborated by the Romance.
brief.zhujiu.skirmish.loss: The cracks in your words reach Cao's mansion first; before the wine is warmed you have become a man under scrutiny.
brief.zhujiu.skirmish.title: Xudu · The Gate Clerk's Questions
brief.zhujiu.skirmish.why: What the gate clerk probes is not your travel papers but whom you have met lately and whom you have saved. Answer too fully, and your hand is shown before the green-plum pavilion even opens.
brief.zhujiu.skirmish.win: You pass the questioning without revealing your purpose and take a seat in the green-plum pavilion; Cao Cao must read you in person, not hear others answer for you.
brief.zhujiu.source: Records of the Three Kingdoms: Biography of the Late Sovereign; Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 21
brief.zuizhong.adaptation: The Writer is a fictional character of the whole book. After the game, sealing the scroll, returning history, and tearing the scroll represent preserving the rewrite, restoring the original record, and accepting the unknown—there is no standard answer.
brief.zuizhong.boss.loss: The rewrite retreats to the margins for now, but your seat is not erased. Once the Lesson remains, you can still come back and ask him again.
brief.zuizhong.boss.title: The Last Page · Gambling with the Narrator
brief.zuizhong.boss.why: He has written everyone's origins, but you will make him bear a choice before an unknown order of cards. Beat him, and you decide who has the right to write this book's ending.
brief.zuizhong.boss.win: Sealing the scroll, returning history, and tearing the scroll are all placed in your hands at once. You may preserve the apocrypha, restore the original fate, or leave the Three Kingdoms without a final draft.
brief.zuizhong.lead: You have read from the Peach Garden to the return to Jin, saved people and seen armies broken. Now the one who always wrote in the margins finally admits it: only you have never asked him who has the right to hold the brush.
brief.zuizhong.record: This page has no verifiable historical event. It gathers the lives, choices, and costs you left on the earlier pages, and makes the narrator himself submit to a rule where no one can know the next card.
brief.zuizhong.skirmish.loss: You are still led by the experience of the old pages, and he lifts his brush to add a word: "again." The last question is temporarily closed.
brief.zuizhong.skirmish.title: Deep in the Tattered Scroll · A Test of the Brush
brief.zuizhong.skirmish.why: The Writer first probes you with familiar old lines, to see whether you only repeat the answers that won before. Pass this skirmish, and he will truly sit down with you.
brief.zuizhong.skirmish.win: The old lines are stripped of their premises; the Writer can no longer excuse his own choices with an omniscient tone. The final table opens to you.
brief.zuizhong.source: The Writer's original · Final chapter of the tattered scroll
ch.baidicheng.boss.name: Heaven's Mandate · The Long Illness
ch.baidicheng.defeat: In the Yong'an Palace, the long night nears its end.
ch.baidicheng.history: The First Ruler entrusted his heir and died in the Yong'an Palace, aged sixty-three.
ch.baidicheng.name: Baidicheng
ch.baidicheng.note: Writer's note: some opponents are not at the table.
ch.baidicheng.omen.1: The Young Lord at His Side
ch.baidicheng.premise: If that deathbed charge had never been spoken.
ch.baidicheng.regret: The entrustment at Baidi: a hero at the end of his road.
ch.baidicheng.skirmish.name: Palace Guard
ch.baidicheng.yeshi: Autumn went, winter came, and the man on the sickbed sat up. The charge was never spoken after all.
ch.baima.boss.name: The Twin Pillars of Hebei
ch.baima.defeat: Hebei's blades too heavy; Baima's wine poured too fast.
ch.baima.history: Guan Yu cut down Yan Liang at Baima and Wen Chou at Yanjin, and lifted the siege of Baima.
ch.baima.name: Baima
ch.baima.note: Writer's note: Hebei's twin walls — one lost to pride, the other to rage.
ch.baima.premise: If that parting toast had been raised to the wrong man.
ch.baima.regret: Yan Liang beheaded, Wen Chou slain: the edge of Yunchang's blade — and the crack between Cao and Liu.
ch.baima.ruleText: Two battles back to back: blades at Baima, horsemen at Yanjin. The wine gets warmed twice.
ch.baima.skirmish.name: Song Xian · Vanguard of Cao's Camp
ch.baima.yeshi: Both lines broken; the wine warmed twice over. Yunchang kept the credit in his heart and the debt in his sleeve.
ch.baimenlou.boss.name: Lü Bu · Cornered Beast
ch.baimenlou.boss.op.0.name: Lü Bu · Cornered Beast
ch.baimenlou.boss.op.1.name: Chen Gong · One Last Scheme
ch.baimenlou.defeat: The rope at White Gate Tower never stopped waiting.
ch.baimenlou.history: Lü Bu begged Xuande for his life; one word from Xuande, and he was strangled at White Gate Tower.
ch.baimenlou.name: White Gate Tower
ch.baimenlou.note: Writer's note: a cornered beast still fights — especially when it's Lü Bu.
ch.baimenlou.premise: If the Marquis of Wen had heeded Chen Gong — once.
ch.baimenlou.regret: The finest under heaven died for refusing to bow his head.
ch.baimenlou.skirmish.name: Gao Shun · Wall-Breaker Corps
ch.baimenlou.yeshi: The Marquis of Wen listened to Chen Gong, abandoned Xiapi, and fled south to Huainan. The realm stayed broken another ten years.
ch.bowang.boss.name: Xiahou Dun
ch.bowang.defeat: The grass on the slope hasn't dried enough to burn.
ch.bowang.history: The strategist's first command: fire on Bowang Slopes, and Xiahou Dun broke.
ch.bowang.name: Bowang Slopes
ch.bowang.note: Writer's note: before the fire — patience.
ch.bowang.premise: If, when the strategist first played with fire, you were the flame itself.
ch.bowang.regret: One fire at Bowang lit the next thirty years.
ch.bowang.skirmish.name: Cao's Vanguard
ch.bowang.yeshi: When the fire rose, you were standing on the slope. The first of the fires burned its way thirty years forward.
ch.caochuan.boss.name: Cao Cao · On the River
ch.caochuan.defeat: No fog on the river; no arrows on the boats.
ch.caochuan.history: Straw boats, borrowed arrows: a hundred thousand in three days.
ch.caochuan.name: Straw Boats
ch.caochuan.note: Writer's note: you are not the only one who cannot see.
ch.caochuan.premise: If, that night on the river, there had been no fog.
ch.caochuan.regret: Arrows borrowed with straw boats — borrowed from the fog, and from nerve.
ch.caochuan.skirmish.name: Cai Zhong · False Deserter
ch.caochuan.yeshi: When the fog thinned, the boats were full. You bowed north across the water: "My thanks for the arrows, Prime Minister."
ch.changban.boss.name: Cao Cao · The Pursuit
ch.changban.boss.op.0.name: Cao Cao · The Pursuit
ch.changban.boss.op.1.name: Xiahou Dun · Arrow and Eye
ch.changban.boss.op.2.name: Zhang He · Master of the Shift
ch.changban.defeat: Before Changban Slopes, men and horses scattered.
ch.changban.history: Zhao Yun charged in and out seven times; Zhang Fei's shout broke Dangyang Bridge.
ch.changban.name: Changban Slopes
ch.changban.note: Writer's note: with nowhere left to retreat, retreat stops being required.
ch.changban.premise: If the roar on Dangyang Bridge had cracked.
ch.changban.regret: Seven charges in and out, one man, one bridge — all of it lone courage.
ch.changban.skirmish.name: Wen Ping · The Pursuit
ch.changban.yeshi: One roar from the bridge, and the water ran backward. The child in his arms slept on, without a scratch.
ch.chencang.boss.name: Hao Zhao · A Thousand Against the Walls
ch.chencang.defeat: Fire arrows off the walls; the ladders burned to the last.
ch.chencang.history: On the second Qishan campaign the Chancellor besieged Chencang; Hao Zhao held out until the grain ran out, and the retreat cut down Wang Shuang.
ch.chencang.name: Chencang
ch.chencang.note: Writer's note: if you can't take the city, take his reason for holding it.
ch.chencang.premise: If the last ladder burned, there was still one letter.
ch.chencang.regret: A thousand men held Chencang; the Chancellor spent twenty days for nothing.
ch.chencang.skirmish.name: Fierce Warrior of Longxi · Wang Shuang
ch.chencang.yeshi: Twenty days without a breach — then a letter came back from inside the city. The gate of Chencang opens next time, on paper.
ch.chibi.boss.name: Cao Cao · The Linked Fleet
ch.chibi.boss.op.0.name: Cao Cao · The Linked Fleet
ch.chibi.boss.op.1.name: Zhou Yu · The Commander
ch.chibi.boss.op.2.name: Zhuge Liang · Borrowing the Wind
ch.chibi.defeat: The southeast wind never rose that night.
ch.chibi.history: The east wind was borrowed; the linked fleet burned; Cao Cao fled down the Huarong Trail.
ch.chibi.name: Red Cliffs
ch.chibi.note: Writer's note: wait for the wind — or force it.
ch.chibi.premise: If, that night, the southeast wind had never risen.
ch.chibi.regret: Eight hundred thousand linked hulls, wagered on one night of east wind.
ch.chibi.ruleText: Three sides at one table, each fighting for himself. The blinds climb faster — clear the table before the fire loses patience.
ch.chibi.skirmish.name: Northern Marines
ch.chibi.yeshi: The wind rose from the tips of the duckweed. By morning, eight hundred thousand linked hulls were ash.
ch.daodan.boss.name: Lu Su · The Feast at Lukou
ch.daodan.defeat: Three rounds of wine — and ambushes on every side.
ch.daodan.history: Lu Su summoned Guan Yu to talks over Jingzhou. One man, one blade; Yu came, laughed, talked, and walked home.
ch.daodan.name: The Single-Blade Meeting
ch.daodan.note: Writer's note: this page is won on reason, not nerve.
ch.daodan.premise: If that blade had truly left its sheath.
ch.daodan.regret: The single-blade meeting was the calmest chance Yunchang ever took.
ch.daodan.skirmish.name: Ambush in the Tent · Ding Feng
ch.daodan.yeshi: The blade never left its sheath, and the words did all the work. Lu Su walked him to the river himself; the quarrel over Jingzhou bought three quiet years.
ch.dingjunshan.boss.name: Xiahou Yuan
ch.dingjunshan.boss.op.0.name: Xiahou Yuan · The Swift Spearhead
ch.dingjunshan.boss.op.1.name: Zhang He · The Patient Counter
ch.dingjunshan.defeat: On Mount Dingjun, the banner snapped.
ch.dingjunshan.history: Huang Zhong cut Xiahou Yuan down in the field; Hanzhong was decided.
ch.dingjunshan.name: Mount Dingjun
ch.dingjunshan.note: Writer's note: hold the high ground, and you hold the momentum.
ch.dingjunshan.premise: If the old general's blade had swung wide.
ch.dingjunshan.regret: Older and stronger: one stroke settled Hanzhong.
ch.dingjunshan.skirmish.name: Veteran of Hanzhong · Guo Huai
ch.dingjunshan.yeshi: The blade fell like thunder and Yuan's army broke on its own. Below the hill, on the white horse, the old general stroked his beard and smiled.
ch.fengyiting.boss.name: Dong Zhuo
ch.fengyiting.boss.op.0.name: Dong Zhuo · Master of Meiwu
ch.fengyiting.boss.op.1.name: Lü Bu · Halberd at the Pavilion
ch.fengyiting.defeat: The honey-trap failed — and the lady paid for it.
ch.fengyiting.history: One halberd from Lü Bu, and the tyrant was dead.
ch.fengyiting.name: Fengyi Pavilion
ch.fengyiting.note: Writer's note: on this page, seeing is not believing.
ch.fengyiting.premise: If the interlocking ruse had come apart in that pavilion.
ch.fengyiting.regret: A honey-trap is a tightrope: one wrong step and the whole board is lost.
ch.fengyiting.ruleText: On this page, seeing is not believing: false tells and feints come double.
ch.fengyiting.skirmish.name: Dong's House Guards
ch.fengyiting.yeshi: The whispers in the pavilion reached the wrong ears. The Grand Tutor suspected nothing. The trap was already set.
ch.ganlu.boss.name: The Blade of Sima Zhao
ch.ganlu.boss.op.0.name: Jia Chong · The Hand on the Blade
ch.ganlu.boss.op.1.name: Sima Zhao · Prince of Jin
ch.ganlu.defeat: The Son of Heaven's blood failed to wake Luoyang.
ch.ganlu.history: Cao Mao marched on Sima Zhao; Jia Chong had Cheng Ji cut him down at the southern gate. Wei survived in name only.
ch.ganlu.name: Ganlu Hall
ch.ganlu.note: Writer's note: the stake on this page isn't the win. It's the record.
ch.ganlu.premise: If the 'Hidden Dragon' poem had been written after the blade left its sheath.
ch.ganlu.regret: Sima Zhao's heart, plain to every passerby; the Son of Heaven's blood, spilled beneath his own carriage.
ch.ganlu.ruleText: He waits for you to show first — the imperial name is your only chip. Don't go all-in.
ch.ganlu.skirmish.name: The Informer's Brush · Wang Shen
ch.ganlu.yeshi: Beneath the southern gate, Cheng Ji's halberd froze in midair. The court historian looked up: "Your Majesty — I write it as it happened."
ch.gaopingling.boss.name: Sima Yi · The Feigned Sickness
ch.gaopingling.defeat: The man who feigned illness beat the man who was truly ill.
